messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 57

The rain that afternoon turns the desert floor into a slick, dark mirror. Elias stands three hundred yards from the suspected device, his hands steady inside the thick rubber gloves, when the secondary trigger fires. It is not an explosion of shrapnel, but a hiss. A canister ruptures, releasing a pale yellow vapor that clings to his visor. He feels the chemical burn before the alarms sound. Inside his suit, the air grows thick and sweet with the smell of almonds and burnt plastic. He pulls his mask tighter, but the seal has already failed. The world blurs. His throat closes. He stumbles backward, coughing until his ribs ache, watching the vapor swallow the convoy. Medics drag him away, but the burn never leaves his lungs. In the weeks that follow, isolation wards and sterile rooms become his reality. The physicians call it a nerve agent exposure, then a blister agent. Elias simply understands it as the day his body stops trusting the air. He returns home to his wife, Amara, who meets him at the door with a damp cloth and a look that never quite settles in her eyes. He sleeps on the couch because the bedroom carries the ghost of his old uniform. He takes hot showers until the water turns cold, scrubbing his skin raw, trying to erase the memory of the visor fogging up. He stops returning to the base. The sight of yellow caution tape makes his stomach turn. He avoids news reports about chemical weapons. He avoids crowded markets. He avoids silence, because silence means he can hear the hiss again. Now, at sixty-two, Elias sits in the clinic chair, his hands resting on his knees. The leather squeaks under his weight, and his shoulders tighten. He describes the morning routine with meticulous care. He checks the window latches three times. He runs the air purifier in every room before Amara wakes. When the wind shifts outside, he stands by the open window just to prove to himself he can breathe. His thoughts spiral when he catches the faint scent of chlorine from a neighbor’s cleaning supplies. He stops breathing for a count of ten, then exhales slowly, as if his lungs have forgotten their rhythm. At night, the humidity in the bedroom makes the air feel heavy. He sleeps with a fan pointed at the doorway, convinced that if the air moves too slowly, it will collect in the corners like it did that day. Amara says he wakes up gasping, his eyes wide, his voice rough from trying to draw in enough oxygen. He still visits the garage most mornings. He says the work keeps him grounded. He polishes old motorcycles, his hands moving with the same precision he once used to cut wires and defuse triggers. But when a wrench drops and clatters on the concrete floor, his shoulders lock. His breath hitches. He bends down too quickly, then stops himself, waiting for the smell, the hiss, the burn. He describes how he watches the horizon when he drives, how he avoids underpasses, how he never travels by air. When his grandchildren visit, he holds them at arm’s length, afraid that their laughter will mimic a detonation and bring it all back. He knows it does not make sense. He knows the air in this room is filtered. He knows he is safe. But his body keeps counting the seconds between breaths, waiting for the gas to find him again.
